Abstract
Background  Understanding social determinants of health is a crucial aspect of holistic healthcare, and cultivating 
empathy toward patients’ suffering is increasingly recognized as a core competency for healthcare professionals. 
Although previous studies have examined the efficacy of narrative medicine-based education in enhancing empathic 
responses to patients, the possibility of learning concept of “social suffering” through patient illness narrative remains 
underexplored.
Methods  This study presents a qualitative analysis of short essays submitted by forty second-year medical students 
at a single medical school after a class based on narrative medicine principle. The students analyzed and interpreted 
a transcript of a patient with hypertension, revealing various dimensions of the illness experience, including 
anxiety regarding the disease, aversion to antihypertensive medications, and encounters with stigmatization and 
discrimination in the workplace. Using an iterative coding process with both inductive and deductive elements, we 
identified patterns in how students conceptualized suffering and engaged with social dimensions of illness.
Results  Our analysis yielded three major themes: (1) categorical framings of suffering, (2) emerging recognition of 
narrative complexity, and (3) limited engagement with structural dimensions of social suffering. While students readily 
identified physical and psychological aspects of suffering, most demonstrated surface-level engagement with social 
dimensions. The students’ responses revealed challenges in moving beyond individualistic frameworks to recognize 
how social, cultural, and institutional factors shape illness experiences in Korean society.
Conclusion  While the narrative medicine approach successfully fostered recognition of suffering’s complexity and 
the importance of empathy, students’ limited engagement with social suffering suggests the need for curricular 
enhancements. We propose a spiral curriculum that progressively deepens students’ understanding of social 
determinants of health, integrates qualitative research methodologies, and explicitly addresses Korean sociocultural 
contexts that shape illness experiences. This approach may better equip future physicians to recognize and address 
social suffering in their clinical practice.
Keywords  Illness narrative, Social suffering, Medical education, Empathy, Narrative medicine, Qualitative research
Learning about social suffering through illness 
narrative: possibilities and challenges
Young-Gyung Paik1 and Jidong Sung2*

Background
Perceiving and appreciating social determinants of health 
is a critical component of holistic healthcare. It is rec­
ommended that education on social determinants of 
health be a standard and compulsory part of the training 
for medical students and other health professionals [1]. 
However, teaching and learning about social determi­
nants of health present challenges in medical education,

primarily due to conceptual complexity and lack of cur­
ricular guidance [2–4]. Various approaches have been 
adopted to integrate social science into medical training 
of students and postgraduate trainees [5–8]. However, 
there is a concern that medical education positions the 
social determinants of health as ‘facts to be known’ rather 
than as ‘conditions to be challenged and changed’ [9]. 
More important than the inclusion of any specific disci­
pline is the creation of an environment in which future 
physicians may be exposed to critical thinking across a 
wide range of themes that characterize the social and cul­
tural context for medical practice [5]. Multidisciplinary 
and inter-faculty courses are fostered and social science 
is one of the essential disciplines to be integrated into the 
curricula [10]. 
On the other hand, empathy towards patients’ suffer­
ing is increasingly recognized as a core competency for 
healthcare professionals [11, 12]. Narrative medicine has 
been proposed as a model for fostering humane medical 
practice through the cultivation of competency of empa­
thy [13]. Although studies have examined the efficacy 
of narrative medicine-based education and training in 
enhancing empathic responses to patients’ suffering [14–
16], ‘social suffering’ has been seldom addressed. The 
term “suffering” lacks a consistent definition; however, 
according to a conceptual framework by Anderson [17] it 
is defined as ‘distress resulting from threat or damage to 
one’s body or self-identity’ encompassing both individual 
(physical and mental) and social dimensions.
The concept of “social suffering” offers a theoretical 
framework that extends beyond individual experiences 
of illness to encompass the structural, political, and cul­
tural dimensions that shape health and illness. As defined 
by Kleinman, Das and Lock [18], social suffering results 
from “what political, economic, and institutional power 
does to people,” with health problems representing one 
manifestation of these broader societal forces. This con­
ceptualization challenges the biomedical model’s ten­
dency to locate suffering primarily within individual 
bodies and minds, highlighting instead how social con­
texts shape illness experiences.
The Korean medical education context presents par­
ticular challenges and opportunities for teaching social 
suffering. Historically shaped by the American medical 
education model, Korean medical training has prioritized 
hierarchical knowledge transmission and biomedical 
expertise. Concurrently, students have progressed 
through an educational system characterized by intense 
competition and limited exposure to the humanities and 
social sciences [19]. Moreover, Korea’s rapid socioeco­
nomic transformation has created unique conditions of 
social suffering, including workplace cultures that pro­
mote long working hours and job-related stress in general 
population, conditions that are also relevant to patient 
populations [20]. These contextual factors make Korea an 
important site for examining how social suffering can be 
taught in medical education.
A study conducted in Brazil [21] reported that an 
internship in primary health care improved sensitivity to 
social suffering through qualitative analyses of the field 
diaries and reports of the interns and transcripts of focus 
group discussion. However explicit pedagogical strate­
gies for developing empathic competencies to address 
patient’s suffering in daily practice were not suggested. 
Similarly, while Wear and Aultman [22] examined medi­
cal students’ resistance to engaging with social inequality 
through literature, their work did not specifically address 
the potential of patient narratives for teaching social suf­
fering. A phenomenological analysis of medical encoun­
ters using the concept of social suffering and narrative 
analysis has been attempted but without consideration 
of medical education [23]. Medical students’ perception 
of their education about suffering was investigated in a 
study using focus group interview, without addressing 
social suffering [24]. 
This study aims to address these gaps by evaluating 
the efficacy of a narrative medicine-based approach in 
improving medical students’ ability to empathize with 
patients’ suffering, with a particular focus on social 
dimensions. By analyzing students’ written reflections 
following engagement with an authentic patient narra­
tive, we explore both the possibilities and challenges of 
teaching social suffering through narrative medicine in a 
Korean medical education context.
Methods
Study design and theoretical framework
This study is a qualitative descriptive study employ­
ing thematic analysis (Braun & Clarke, 2006) to exam­
ine short essays written by medical students following a 
narrative medicine-based class. Our analytical approach 
combined elements of both inductive and deductive rea­
soning. Initially, we used an inductive approach to iden­
tify emergent patterns in students’ conceptualizations 
of suffering. As analysis progressed, we incorporated

deductive elements by using the theoretical framework of 
social suffering [18] to interpret these patterns, particu­
larly focusing on students’ engagement with structural 
and cultural dimensions of illness.

Paik and Sung BMC Medical Education          (2025) 25:978 
This methodological approach aligns with what Max­
well [25] describes as an “interactive” qualitative design, 
where research questions, data collection, and analysis 
procedures evolve through constant interaction. Our 
aim was not simply to categorize student responses but 
to understand how they made meaning of suffering in 
relation to the broader sociocultural context and medical 
education. Our study is positioned within an interpre­
tive/constructivist paradigm, which assumes that reality 
is socially constructed and that understanding emerges 
through interpretation of participants’ meanings and 
experiences. More specifically, our theoretical frame­
work draws from: (1) Social constructionism - We exam­
ine how medical students construct their understanding 
of suffering through social and educational contexts. (2) 
Critical pedagogy in medical education - We explore how 
traditional biomedical education shapes (and potentially 
limits) students’ capacity to recognize social dimensions 
of suffering. (3) The concept of “social suffering” as out­
lined in the Background section. [18]. 
Participants and educational context
Participants are all the second-year medical students 
(forty students) in a single medical school (Sungkyunk­
wan University School of Medicine, Suwon, Kyunggi-do, 
Republic of Korea). The students participated in a class 
which is a part of a compulsory pre-clinical curriculum 
titled ‘Patients and Doctor’, which focuses on basic clini­
cal skills. The two-hour class had an aim of enhancing 
the competency in empathizing with patient’s suffering. 
The class structure is shown in the Table 1. Pre-class indi­
vidual observation activity involved of making notes on 
patient’s suffering after observing an image of a patient 
undergoing respirator treatment via tracheostomy in 
the intensive care unit. This activity was repeated at the 
end of the class as reflection of the class. Students’ notes 
made in this activity were not analyzed in this study. The 
introductory lecture emphasized on the importance of 
addressing social suffering alongside physical and mental 
suffering. As the main content of the class, the students 
read and analyze a transcript of an in-depth interview 
of a hypertensive patient, at first individually, then dis­
cussed in small group and finally shared by the whole 
group. The transcript was printed on paper and cod­
ing was facilitated using re-adhesive paper notes. Stu­
dents were asked to analyze the narrative using a coding 
approach derived from qualitative analysis, first individu­
ally and then through group discussion, with the goal of 
eliciting themes regarding patient’s suffering.
The transcript used for this exercise captured various 
aspects of the patient’s experience with hypertension, 
including symptoms, anxiety regarding potential com­
plications, aversion to antihypertensive medications, and 
experiences of stigmatization and discrimination in the 
workplace. This transcript was previously analyzed in 
a published study [26], which highlighted the suffering 
associated with both individual and social dimensions 
of the illness experience. Specifically, the transcript illus­
trated social suffering through a vignette in which the 
patient concealed his diagnosis from colleagues due to 
fear of stigma and its potential impact on his professional 
trajectory, perceiving the illness as a weakness that might 
undermine confidence in his job performance.
This study was approved by the Institutional Review 
Board of Samsung Medical Center, Seoul, Republic of 
Korea. (IRB no. 2010-03-049). Written informed consent 
was obtained from each student prior to the class. No 
student refused to participate the study.
Data collection
The class took place on June 20, 2019. Following the 
class, students were instructed to submit short essays 
that reflected their insight from the class. The following 
points were provided to guide their writing:
1)	 What is suffering experienced by patients?
2)	 If your perspective of suffering changed after the 
class, how has it changed?
3)	 What do you think doctors should do to resolve or 
alleviate patient’s suffering?
All 40 students submitted essays until 26th, July 2019 in 
electronic format (MS Word files) as a reflecting notes, 
which was not evaluated for students’ grading.
Data analysis
We employed a rigorous, multi-stage process of thematic 
analysis: [27]
1. Familiarization: Both authors independently read all 
essays multiple times to gain familiarity with the content.

2. Initial coding: The corresponding author (J.S.) con­
ducted line-by-line coding of the essays, focusing on how

students defined suffering, their recognition of its mul­
tiple dimensions (particularly social suffering), and their 
proposed approaches as future doctors.
3. Theme development: Both authors collaboratively 
reviewed the initial codes, identifying patterns and rela­
tionships. This process involved regular meetings to dis­
cuss emerging themes and resolve discrepancies through 
consensus.
4. Theme refinement: Themes were continuously 
refined through an iterative process, comparing emerging 
themes against the original data to ensure they accurately 
represented students’ perspectives.
5. Final analysis: The refined themes were analyzed in 
relation to the theoretical framework of social suffering, 
examining the depth of students’ engagement with struc­
tural and cultural dimensions of illness.
Coding and thematic categorization were conducted 
with Atlas.ti 9.1.6.0 Windows (ATLAS.ti Scientific Soft­
ware Development GmbH, Germany).
Quotations were selected from the texts to illustrate 
and justify the study findings. Translations from Korean 
to English were performed and reviewed by both authors, 
and edited by a professional English editing service. Back 
translation was done and the results were reviewed and 
the necessary adjustments were made by the authors. 
Students were identified by participant numbers. Brack­
ets were used to indicate explanatory comments added 
by the authors for clarity and ellipses to denote omitted 
text.
Ensuring rigor and trustworthiness
To enhance the trustworthiness of our analysis, we 
employed several strategies recommended by Lincoln 
and Guba [28]:
1. Investigator triangulation: Both authors, with 
different disciplinary backgrounds, participated in 
data analysis, bringing multiple perspectives to the 
interpretation.
2. Reflexivity: We maintained awareness of our posi­
tionality throughout the analysis. The corresponding 
author (J.S.) is a male clinician trained as a cardiologist, 
who currently works as a preventive cardiologist spe­
cializing in hypertension management and cardiac reha­
bilitation, with additional training in public health. As 
a professor in the medical school teaching medical stu­
dents, he occupies a position where the study results have 
direct implications for his practice. The first author (Y.P.) 
is a female anthropologist with expertise in qualitative 
research, particularly medical anthropology, who main­
tained a more objective position as an observer from out­
side the medical field.
3. Thick description: We provide detailed context 
about the educational setting and substantial quotations 
from student essays to allow readers to evaluate the 
transferability of findings.
4. Negative case analysis: We actively sought and 
incorporated examples that did not fit with emerging pat­
terns to develop a more nuanced analysis.
Results
Our analysis identified three major themes that charac­
terize students’ engagement with the concept of suffer­
ing following the narrative medicine class: (1) categorical 
framings of suffering, (2) emerging recognition of narra­
tive complexity, and (3) limited engagement with struc­
tural dimensions of social suffering. These themes reveal 
both the possibilities and limitations of using narrative 
medicine to teach about social suffering in a Korean 
medical education context. 
Theme 1: Categorical Framings of Suffering
Most students approached suffering through categorical 
frameworks, attempting to classify different dimensions 
of patient experience. The most common pattern was a 
dichotomous framing that separated physical and psy­
chological suffering:
“[My] perspective of patients’ suffering have been 
widened [by the class]. I could have simply recall 
physical pain caused by diseases… But after the 
class, I could recall the other aspect, which is psycho­
logical suffering caused by anxiety of anticipating 
inability to do economic activity or [altered] family 
relationship, in addition to suffering by [physical] 
symptoms. (#35)
This dichotomous framing reflects the persistence of 
Cartesian mind-body dualism in students’ thinking, 
despite the introductory lecture’s emphasis on multi-
dimensional suffering. The dominance of this binary 
framework suggests how deeply biomedical models have 
shaped students’ conceptual schemas, creating challenges

for recognizing the integrated nature of suffering across 
physical, psychological, and social domains.
Some students attempted more complex categoriza­
tions proposing a temporal framework that distinguished 
“primary” from “secondary” suffering:
“Patients’ suffering can be largely divided into two 
categories: primary suffering which is caused by the 
disease with physical manifestation and the patient 
feels secondary suffering indirectly caused by the dis­
ease.” (#2).
This temporal framing, while still categorical and dichot­
omous, demonstrates an emerging recognition of suffer­
ing’s processual nature. However, it continues to position

disease as the primary causal factor, overlooking how 
social conditions might precede and shape both illness 
and the response to illness.
A minority of students recognized iatrogenic suffer­
ing—pain and distress caused by medical interventions 
and interactions:
“What struck me most about the interview script 
was the patient’s anger towards the doctor’s attitude, 
which fostered distrust and aversion to medical 
practice. I realized how doctor-patient relationship 
give new suffering to a patient.” (#12).
These reflections represent an important step toward 
critical self-awareness within the medical profession. By 
acknowledging that medical practice itself can generate 
suffering, these students began to question the assumed 
benevolence of medical interventions. However, even 
these more critical reflections tended to focus on indi­
vidual doctor-patient interactions rather than addressing 
how institutional structures and power differentials in 
healthcare systems contribute to iatrogenic suffering.
Theme 2: emerging recognition of narrative complexity
The second theme captures students’ growing apprecia­
tion for narrative approaches to understanding suffer­
ing. There were students emphasized the importance of 
empathy, and some of them specifically noting the value 
of attentive listening:
“Appreciation and empathy to patient’s complaints 
is not only meaningful in itself, but a good start for a 
solution for the suffering.” (#27).
These comments suggest that engagement with patient 
narratives fostered recognition of empathic commu­
nication as a core clinical skill rather than an optional 
supplement to technical competence. However, the fram­
ing of empathy remained largely instrumental—a “start 
for a solution”—rather than reflecting deeper engage­
ment with the ethical dimensions of bearing witness to 
suffering.
A smaller number of students began to question the 
traditional problem-solving approach to doctor-patient 
relationships:
“I guess I thought that ‘I, as a doctor, am a person 
who should resolve the suffering of the patient’ before 
the class. But now I am thinking that a good doctor 
should think more elaborate thought. Patient’s suf­
fering is surely a subject of doctor’s problem solving. 
But before that, and above that, we should under­
stand it.” (#1).
This reflection represents a significant shift from the hier­
archical, solution-oriented model that dominates Korean 
medical education toward a more collaborative relation­
ship that begins with understanding the patient’s lived 
experience. The student recognizes that understanding 
precedes intervention, suggesting a more patient-cen­
tered approach to clinical practice.
Several students incorporated personal experiences to 
deepen their understanding:
“When it comes to my story, I had experienced some 
chronic diseases myself but the physical pain from 
it is rather endurable. What makes more miserable 
is that the depressive thoughts– ‘Why did I get this 
disease?’ and ‘What will others think of me in this 
condition?’.” (#6).
These reflections demonstrate how narrative approaches 
can activate students’ own illness experiences as 
resources for understanding patient suffering. By con­
necting professional learning with personal experience, 
students began to bridge the divide between clinical 
objectivity and empathic engagement.
Theme 3: limited engagement with structural dimensions 
of social suffering
Despite explicit instruction on social suffering, students’ 
engagement with structural and cultural dimensions 
remained limited. Some students mentioned “labeling 
effects,” recognizing how disease diagnosis affects social 
identity:
“Nailing down oneself to being ‘a patient’ may easily 
results in self-restriction and lowered self-esteem…” 
(#24).
While these reflections acknowledge the social impli­
cations of illness identity, they frame the issue primar­
ily in psychological terms—how individuals internalize 
labels—rather than examining the social processes that 
create and enforce these labels. The analysis remains at 
the level of individual experience rather than addressing 
the cultural meanings attached to illness in Korean soci­
ety or how these meanings are shaped by broader social 
structures.
A minority of students discussed the ‘social’ factors 
that may lead to patient’s suffering, in superficial ways in 
most cases
“A patient has many sufferings other than the main

symptom of the disease. Psychological suffering 
caused by a thought of becoming a patient, socially 
experienced suffering, suffering as a result of the lack

Paik and Sung BMC Medical Education          (2025) 25:978 
of communication with the medical professionals…” 
(#3).
These comments acknowledge social dimensions of suf­
fering but treat them as secondary consequences of dis­
ease rather than examining how social conditions shape 
the experience and meaning of illness itself. Students 
recognized discrimination in the workplace but did not 
analyze how Korean workplace culture—with its empha­
sis on dedication, overtime work, and after-hours social­
izing—creates particular vulnerabilities for patients with 
chronic conditions.
A small number of students mentioned economic 
factors:
“To make things simple, it can be summarized to 
money and human relationship. The cost of treating 
a disease is not negligible. We have universal health 
insurance but… in case of a disease which warrants 
surgery, it may cost a lot.” (#28).
While acknowledging the financial burden, these reflec­
tions did not engage with the political economy of 
healthcare in Korea or question how economic inequali­
ties structure access to care. The issue was framed as an 
individual financial challenge rather than a manifestation 
of structural inequities.
A few students briefly noted stigmatization:
“Even if a patient was cured of cancer and living a 
normal life, a look of pity is unavoidable when it was 
revealed that he/she was a cancer patient.” (#22).
These observations recognize stigma but do not analyze 
its cultural foundations or how it reflects power rela­
tions in society. Students noted the existence of “social 
prejudice” but did not explore how Korean cultural val­
ues around productivity, family responsibility, and social 
harmony might intensify stigma for people with chronic 
conditions.
Very small number of students attempted deeper 
engagement with social dimensions:
“A doctor has limitation in resolving the patient’s 
suffering stemming from social prejudice. Social 
suffering such as this may be caused by regulation 
in workplace and social atmosphere but also by 
patient’s intimidation in the social relationship with 
the people around. This case in the class was diag­
nosed of hypertension which is very common nowa­
days, and had big worries and intimidated by the 
thought that he may have disadvantage and unfa­
vorable social relationship. It would be helpful to 
patients if [doctors] provide reasonable explanation 
of the disease and good communication… so that 
patients can confidently maintain social relation­
ship and avoid social withdrawal.” (#4).
This reflection approaches a structural analysis by 
acknowledging workplace regulations and social atmo­
sphere as sources of suffering. However, the proposed 
solution—better communication from doctors—returns 
to an individual-level intervention rather than addressing 
the need for structural changes in workplace policies or 
public health education.
Another student noted:
“The most impressive point I observed in the class is 
that worries and concerns related to the social situ­
ation may be the worst suffering caused by a disease. 
I have not felt or considered such a feeling even when 
I was a patient myself. Maybe that’s because I have 
not been responsible for a family or a duty in the 
workplace.” (#30).
This reflection demonstrates emerging awareness of how 
social roles and responsibilities shape the experience of 
illness, recognizing that workplace and family obliga­
tions in Korean society create particular vulnerabilities. 
However, even this more nuanced analysis does not fully 
engage with how these responsibilities are structured by 
gender norms, economic pressures, and cultural expecta­
tions in contemporary Korean society.
Discussion
This qualitative study analyzed short essays written by 
students following a class designed to cultivate empathy 
for patients’ suffering through the principles of narrative 
medicine. The analysis indicates that the primary learn­
ing objectives of the class were largely met. The students 
appreciated that: (1) patient’s suffering is not just equal 
to physical pain but also includes sufferings from various 
sources including psychological suffering, (2) empathy is 
an essential aspect of medical practice and just treating 
patient’s disease by biomedical approach would be often 
inadequate in dealing with patient’s suffering.
From individual to structural understanding: challenges in 
teaching social suffering
Our findings highlight a persistent tendency among stu­
dents to individualize suffering, framing it primarily in 
terms of physical symptoms and psychological responses 
rather than analyzing its social determinants. Even when 
students acknowledged social factors such as workplace 
discrimination or stigma, they often treated these as 
secondary consequences of disease rather than exam­
ining how social conditions fundamentally shape the 
experience and meaning of illness. This individualistic

Paik and Sung BMC Medical Education          (2025) 25:978 
framing reflects what Farmer [29] describes as the “deso­
cialization” of suffering in biomedical discourse, which 
abstracts illness from its social context and locates it pri­
marily within individual bodies and minds. The research 
previously published by the authors [26] discussed this 
issue based on the same patient’s transcripts and high­
lighted how workplace culture, including after-hours 
gatherings and demanding working conditions, contrib­
uted to the patient’s decision to conceal his hypertension, 
ultimately leading to job changes. Such contextual analy­
sis is vital for understanding the multifaceted nature of 
social suffering.
Studies in the field of medical education have rarely 
addressed social suffering. One study of a literature 
course about family values for fourth-year medical stu­
dents reported students’ resistance to course material 
and discussions related to sexual identity and non-tradi­
tional family values, male-female relationships, and white 
racism - i.e., oppressive social structures that sustain suf­
fering [22]. Compared to this work using literature as 
course materials, our study addressed a real patient’s nar­
rative. While variety in class material is important, actual 
patients’ narratives can provide more vivid reflections of 
reality.
Several limitations may account for students’ challenges 
in analyzing social suffering more thoroughly. First, med­
ical curricula typically prioritize biomedical knowledge, 
reflecting the legacy of the Flexner Report that influ­
enced Korean medical education shaping its curriculum 
[30]. Intensive study of the biomedical sciences remains 
a core component of undergraduate medical education. 
Such immersive curricula can foster strong identification 
with biomedicine among students, often at the expense 
of broader perspectives on health and disease [31]. While 
there is growing interest in social determinants of health 
in medical education, its curricular dissemination is still 
limited and existing program show heterogeneity and 
scarcity of objective assessments [2]. 
Second, study participants have never had a training of 
qualitative analysis and narrative medicine. While they 
already have been exposed to epidemiology and medical 
statistics, i.e., quantitative research methods, they had 
no experience in qualitative analysis of texts before and 
after this class. This gap is not unique to this cohort but 
reflects a broader trend in medical education worldwide 
[16, 32]. 
Medical professionals trained in such environments 
may demonstrate a limited understanding of, or even 
skepticism toward, qualitative research methodologies. 
Among the peer review comments on previously pub­
lished work by the authors [26] using qualitative analysis, 
one reviewer dismissed qualitative approaches entirely: 
“The qualitative design is not at all appropriate for this 
study… there is little evidence globally of stigma and 
discrimination experienced by patients with hyperten­
sion.” [33] The provision of medical education and health 
care should be based on a critical understanding of the 
nature of knowledge itself, and epistemological discus­
sion for various research paradigms is important not only 
for researchers but also for medical students [34]. 
Third, as pre-clinical students, the study participants 
had limited practical experience in clinical settings. 
While some attempted to relate their personal experi­
ences with patients (e.g., family members), the absence 
of direct clinical encounters significantly constrained 
their understanding of suffering. Moreover, as college 
students, they have limited social experience, with issues 
such as social prejudices toward chronic diseases and 
workplace cultures invloving long working hours or after-
hour gatherings, which were discussed in the previous 
study by the authors [26]. The limited clinical and social 
experience of students resulted in constraints on the level 
of complexity they could achieve in addressing the issue, 
which warrants a spiral curriculum as shown in the next 
subsection.
Toward a spiral curriculum for teaching social suffering
A single class is likely to be insufficient to deepen stu­
dents’ understanding of social suffering beyond individ­
ual empathy. Concerns have been raised that healthcare 
providers’ empathy tends to decline throughout training, 
and a spiral curriculum, a curriculum design in which 
key concept are presented repeatedly with deepening 
complexity, is recommended as a potential remedy to 
maintain empathetic engagement [35, 36]. To enhance 
appreciation of social suffering, a specially designed cur­
riculum that employs a spiral approach with incremental 
emphasis on social determinants of health is warranted 
[7]. 
A spiral curriculum for teaching social suffering might 
include:
1. Foundation stage: Introduction to narrative medi­
cine and basic concepts of social suffering through analy­
sis of patient narratives (similar to the class analyzed in 
this study).
2. Theoretical deepening: Integration of social science

perspectives from medical anthropology, sociology, and 
political economy to provide analytical tools for under­
standing structural dimensions of suffering.
3. Methodological training: Introduction to qualita­
tive research methods to enhance students’ capacity to 
analyze narrative data and recognize patterns beyond 
individual experience.
4. Contextual application: Case-based learning that 
explicitly addresses how Korean social structures— 
including workplace culture, family systems, and gender 
norms—shape illness experiences.

Paik and Sung BMC Medical Education          (2025) 25:978 
5. Clinical integration: Supervised clinical experiences 
that encourage students to identify and address social 
suffering in real patient encounters, with structured 
reflection on structural interventions.
This spiral approach would allow for progressive devel­
opment of critical consciousness about social suffering, 
moving from recognition to analysis to intervention. By 
integrating theoretical perspectives with practical expe­
riences, it could help students develop both the analyti­
cal tools to understand social suffering and the practical 
skills to address it in clinical practice.
Recent study highlighted the helplessness and burn-out 
experienced by physicians who realized their minimal 
ability to influence the underpinning social determinants 
of health [37]. A medical curriculum addressing social 
suffering should incorporate practical coping strategy 
which can be applied in real-world practice, rather than 
solely focusing on raising awareness and empathy for 
patients’ suffering.
Limitations and future directions
This study has several limitations. As a single-institution 
study in Korea, the findings may not be generalizable to 
other cultural or educational contexts. The analysis relied 
on written reflections rather than direct observation of 
learning or longitudinal assessment of attitudinal change, 
limiting our understanding of how students’ perspectives 
evolved over time. Additionally, our focus on a narrative 
medicine class addressing a specific chronic condition 
(hypertension) may not capture the full range of chal­
lenges in teaching about social suffering related to other 
health conditions.
Future research should explore longitudinal impacts of 
narrative medicine on students’ understanding of social 
suffering, examine how different pedagogical approaches 
might enhance engagement with structural dimensions, 
and investigate the influence of cultural contexts on 
receptivity to social suffering concepts. Cross-cultural 
comparative studies could provide valuable insights into 
how different educational and healthcare systems shape 
students’ engagement with social suffering.
Conclusion
While our narrative medicine-based class successfully 
enhanced students’ recognition of suffering’s complex­
ity and the importance of empathy in medical practice, 
it did not fully achieve the goal of developing students’ 
understanding of social suffering. Most students’ engage­
ment with social dimensions remained superficial, lack­
ing critical analysis of the structural and cultural factors 
that shape illness experiences in Korean society.
These findings highlight both the potential and limita­
tions of narrative medicine for teaching social suffering. 
While patient narratives can disrupt symptom-centered 
approaches and foster empathic engagement, additional 
pedagogical elements are needed to develop students’ 
capacity for structural analysis and intervention.
We propose a spiral curriculum that progressively 
deepens students’ engagement with social suffer­
ing through integration of social science perspectives, 
methodological training, contextual application, and 
clinical integration. By combining narrative approaches 
with structural analysis and practical strategies, medical 
education can better prepare students to recognize and 
address the social dimensions of suffering in their future 
clinical practice.
